Maij 1733. groot agtb: voor den sulthan akomoedin hadden gerigt, hebben wij den 21. ' maart onder het afleggen van uwel Edelen groot agtb: minissame groete dien vorst g'intrageert, dog over geensakelijkheden diertijd gehandeld; maar op een nader oudientie bij dien majesteijt over den peper handel sprekende, alsoo een groote quantiteijt in de omleggende negorije in gereetheijt was, die wij versogt en aan d' Ecomp:e alleen gelevert souden werden, waar op dien koning soo het ons toescheen niet regt sijnen mening dorst uijt en en, niet anders dan dubbelsinnig antwoord gaff en niets tot versekering van den handel konden ontwaren, dierhalven vervoegden wij ons na pangerang proboe anum die wij den mening van uwel Edelen groot agtb: in ernstige termen van den peper alleen 'temogen hebben voorsloegen, die ons randborstig antwoorden daar moeten twee wankang off Jonken meede geladen werden en men sal een schip van d' Eecomp:e ook van peper besorgen, het Jagt de vriendschap ende 24 p=s snaphanen voor reecq: van desen vorst mede gebragt,
text_translated_detailed:
From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1733. Batavia. To His Excellency, a Most Noble and Esteemed Lord, Mr. Dirk van Cloon, Governor General, and the Noble Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Most Noble and Esteemed, Great and Honored: Earnest, Valiant, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords.

Received on the 25th of May 1733.

After we had obtained our orders from Your Excellency's Great Honor, we departed on the 9th of March last with the ship Westerbeek [ship name] under sail, in the company of the yacht De Vriendschap [The Friendship], and the Tanjongvouren, the Onbeschaamtheid [The Shamelessness], and the Kranke [The Sick], which arrived together with us on the 22nd of that date before the river of Banjarmasin, which we first sailed up with those small boats and arrived before the village of Tatas on the 26th of the same month. The letter and gift goods which Your Excellency's Great Honor had directed for the Sultan Akomoddin, we delivered on the 21st of March while presenting Your Excellency's Great Honor's most amiable greetings to that prince, though no business matters were handled at that time. But upon a later audience with that Majesty concerning the pepper trade, since a great quantity was in readiness in the surrounding villages, which we requested and would be delivered to the Company alone, the king did not seem to dare to express his true meaning clearly, but gave only ambiguous answers and we could discern nothing to secure the trade. Therefore we betook ourselves to Pangeran Praboe Anum, to whom we proposed Your Excellency's Great Honor's meaning in earnest terms regarding pepper alone, who answered us somewhat reluctantly that two wankangs [type of vessel] or junks must be loaded alongside, and the Company's ship shall also be provided with pepper. The yacht De Vriendschap and 24 pieces of muskets for the account of this prince were also brought,

We have been informed here from the side that the pepper crop of the previous year has been very good, for in the uplands and the surrounding villages there is well 15,000 picols in stock, of which we shall obtain the smallest quantity to our sorrow. We have been brought 70,000 pounds of pepper which have been loaded in the ship Westerbeek, and now most of the Chinese and native merchants are bringing that Chinese junk which we found here before Tatas upon our arrival, which will be able to depart from here with a quantity of 12 to 13,000 picols, which will considerably reduce the stock, and it is to be feared that the ship Westerbeek will not be able to obtain a full cargo within two or three months. The pepper harvest of this year stands to this day in poor condition due to the continuing rain that has fallen here, and it is thought that little of that green pepper of this monsoon will be able to be obtained, which we leave to the wiser judgment of Your Excellency's Great Honor whether such can be relied upon, to prevent the great losses that could be caused by the delivery of goods again. Regarding the two pepper scales which were also given by Your Excellency's Great Honor for the weighing of that pepper, they are of no use here, although we have sought to obtain such through earnest and persistent requests to the king and prince, it has been fruitless. We have until now not been able to discern that the king and prince are well disposed toward the Company, for they prefer to sell their goods to foreign merchants rather than to the Company, which is evident from the fact that previously they always had a proclamation circulated to make known to the inhabitants that their pepper would be delivered to the Company alone. This has not yet occurred to this day, which is indeed a principal reason why we have collected so little pepper until now and our fear is that in this monsoon not more than one ship's cargo of dry pepper will be able to be obtained. The officers of the ship Westerbeek have properly delivered their cargo, except that in case number 40, in which were enclosed 24 pieces of muskets, we found only 23 pieces, and since those firearms were destined for the account of the Sultan, we have taken one firearm from that hold to make up for the shortage, of which we hope to obtain a favorable approval from Your Excellency's Great Honor, whose pious and weighty concerns we in all holy reverence have commended. We remain with deep respect, Most Noble, Esteemed, and Widely Commanding Lords, Your High Excellency's obedient and humble servants. [Signed] C. De Marre and D. Brouwer. From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1733. Banjarmasin in the village Tatas.

The 2nd of May, in the Year 1733. Batavia. To His Excellency, Most Noble and Esteemed Lord Dirk van Cloon, Governor General, and the Noble Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Most Noble and Esteemed, Great and Honored: Earnest, Valiant, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords.

Our humble letters of the 2nd of the past month of May we hope will have been received well by Your High Excellency, of which this is a duplicate, wherein we have communicated to Your High Excellency's Great Honor that we had purchased 50,000 pounds of pepper, which quantity has only been increased to 172,012 pounds, which we have obtained with much effort and continual requests to the Sultan, Pangeran, and those who are appointed for this purpose in this village, from one another. Of these, two of the three Chinese junks have been fully loaded and have already departed, the last shall also undertake its journey within a few days.

text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1723. Brouwer /in margin/ Banjarmasin in the Negeri Tatas, the 2nd of May, Year 1723.— Batavia. To His Excellency, the Most Esteemed, High and Noble, Strict Lord Dirk van Cloon, Governor General, and the Noble Lords, Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Most High and Noble, Strict, Great and Esteemed, Earnest, Faithful, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords. We hope that our humble letters of the 2nd of the past month of May will have been received well by Your High Excellencies, of which this is a duplicate, wherein we have communicated to Your High Excellencies that we had purchased 50,000 pounds of pepper, which quantity has only increased to 172,012 pounds, which we have obtained with much effort and continual requests from the Sultan, the Pangeran, and those appointed in this negeri [settlement], whereby two of the three Chinese junks have been fully loaded and have already departed, the last one shall also undertake its journey within a few days. Banjarmasin, the 11th of June 1733. Regarding the pepper trade for the Esteemed Company, to have it exclusively from these lands, we regard as an impossible matter, for although the Sultan and Prince Praboe Anum keep us occupied with promises and provide assurances in their letters to Your High Excellencies, their powers in execution do not prove sufficient, partly due to the disloyalty of their trusted servants, who allow themselves to be easily corrupted, and on the other hand, the enmity in which the princes commonly live, and those who will not observe any order from the king, and brings then, on account of the higher price that the Chinese pay for pepper, their goods to the same, which gives a foothold so that the common subjects follow, imagining themselves just as well as a pangeran [prince] to be able to transgress the orders, for which no punishment is administered,

text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin, the 1st of June 1733. Extract from the Banjarmasin daily register, dated the 7th of June 1733. Toward evening one of the pepper writers came to tell us that Pangerang Prabanum wished to give us a visit at seven o'clock, which we granted to that Prince. We were of the opinion that he had an important reason to communicate it to us, because he had chosen such an inconvenient hour for it. That Prince appeared at the appointed time with a small retinue, as we had requested. We offered him tea, betel nut, and so forth. During this refreshment, that Prince asked us whether we wished to depart with the ship and Tanjongpoura soon. We answered that we would remain when pepper could be obtained in this territory. That Prince replied that there is little pepper left, and I fear that this year with the new pepper we shall not have more than the ship can load. He expressed to us that he is very much concerned for the Honored Company, and that he and the King would send a letter to the Governor-General in which they promised to deliver the pepper solely to the Honored Company. To this we replied that the Governor-General and the Council of India are qualified to make a contract with the King and all the Princes, excluding all others. And that when the King and Princes might resolve to do so, it must be stipulated that when anyone from this land wished to export pepper, the Honored Company would be free to seize it and confiscate it, or else divide it, one half for the King and the other half for the Honored Company. text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin, the 1st of August 1733. High Noble, strict, greatly esteemed, most earnest, most wise, most prudent, and very generous lords. Our letters of the 11th of June of the previous year have, we trust, been delivered to your High Excellency in due time, whose duplicates extracted from the daily register of this [office] are enclosed herewith. And we have not without reason shared with your High Excellency our thoughts regarding a shortage of pepper to our regret in the previous letters, for with our last dispatch there was shipped in the ship Westerbeek 17,201½ pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 7,800 kg]. Since that time purchased 43,449 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 19,700 kg], so that the cargo loaded in the aforementioned vessel amounts to 245,461 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 111,300 kg] of pepper. Dirk van lloon gouverneur Generaal, ende de Edele heeren Raden van Nederlands India Hoog Edele gestrenge groot Agtb=r Erntfeste Manhafte, Wel Wijse voorsienige en seer genereuse heeren. — sedert onse Laatste Eerbiedige Letteren van 10. deser welkers dupplicaat nevens desen is g'jncuseert hebben wij eenlijk kennen bemagtigen 17929. lb peper 't geen een getiige quantiteijt is in dese tijd, daar dien Corl thans in abondantie behoorden te werden afgebragt, alsoo het gewas van dit voorjaar reets bij de bepoters is opgelegt, die het selve niet minder willen verkoopen als voor de prijs daar sij dat graan voor hebben verdebiteerd ten tijden der Ionken, en alsoo onse ordres van uw hoog Ed: groot agtb:r sijn tot 4 realen en ¼ d=o thol voor het picol te besteden, tot welke minderen prijs de volkeren hier niet Van Banjermassing den 29:' aug:s 1733. genegen sijn na de boven negorije te vaaren om de peper van daar af te brengen, alsoo die betuijgen geen voordeelen te kenne behalen maar nodeloose koste te moeten doen, door de hooge markt, dog wanneer den Zulthan en pangerang praboe anum nu haaren ijver en genegentheijt wille betoonen voor d' E: Comp: soude deselve daar in ordere stellen en de volkeren van de boven negorije ordonneeren de peper te verkoopen gelijk in voorige Jaaren, en wel principaal in 1727. en 28. is gedaan, dat de afbrengers soude aanmoedigen om de reijse te doen, gelijk op die tijd gebleken is, want toen een kloeke quantiteijt is bemagtigt geworden. dese besluijte na uw hoog Ed: groot Agtb„r in Godes hoede bevolen te hebbe neemen de vrijheijt ons te noemen /onderstond/ hoog Ed: gestrenge en wijt gebiedende heeren /:lager/ Uw hoog Edelens gehoorsame en onderdanige dienaaren
text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin on the 29th of August 1733.— To Batavia. To His Excellency the highly noble and esteemed Lord Mr. Dirk van Illon, Governor General, and the noble gentlemen Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Highly noble, esteemed, great and worthy, earnest, steadfast, wise, prudent and most generous gentlemen.— Since our last respectful letters of the 10th of this month, whose duplicate is enclosed herewith, we have only been able to procure 17,929 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 8,100 kg] of pepper, which is a meager quantity at this time, whereas this commodity should now be brought in abundance, since the harvest from this past spring has already been delivered to the traders, who are unwilling to sell it for less than the price at which they purchased that grain during the time of the junks, and whereas our orders from your high Excellency are to spend 4 reals and a quarter [modern equivalent: a specific currency unit of the period] per picul [modern equivalent: approximately 61 kg], to which lower price the peoples here are not willing to travel to the aforementioned village to bring pepper from there, as they claim they can gain no advantage but must incur needless costs due to the high market prices. However, if the Sultan and Pangeran Praboe Anum now wish to demonstrate their zeal and goodwill toward the Esteemed Company, they would arrange matters and order the peoples of the aforementioned village to sell pepper as in previous years, and particularly as was done in 1727 and 1728, so that the transporters would be encouraged to make the journey, as was evident at that time, for then a considerable quantity was obtained. This matter we commend to your high Excellency in God's keeping, and take the liberty to name ourselves, with respect, your high Excellency's esteemed and widely commanding gentlemen. Your high Excellency's obedient and humble servants.

text_translated_detailed: Regarding this trade matter, please be informed that a duplicate letter was sent from here to Your High Excellency, greatly honored, on the 29th of August of this year, along with four muster rolls such as were conducted here under the final [month] of June. We shall not fail to observe Your High Excellency's greatly honored commands to depart from here before the blowing of the west winds, and we have informed the king and pangerang [regent] accordingly, who will have a letter ready by the 10th of the coming month to be conveyed to Your High Excellency by us, after whose receipt we shall undertake the journey with the ship and Tanjongpourais [Tanjung Pura] with all speed. The pepper collected has amounted to 250,538 pounds, and we have received 945 Spanish reals [Spanish currency] on account of the king's debt, of which the remainder is still 141 reals and 50 [centavos]. We hope to see this also settled before our departure, as the sultan has assured us he will send it. Thus we conclude, commending Your High Excellency to God's protection, remaining with deep respect. [Undersigned] Your High Excellency's obedient and humble servants [was signed] C. de Marre and D. text_translated_detailed: Company in friendship, and to make their subjects understand the following commands, and to compel them to obedience thereof, and also that this Contract shall be observed by all their descendants, and for eternal remembrance the same shall be engraved in copper as an eternal memorial of imperishability. — The Company shall annually tolerate as many junks here for trade in the sale of Chinese goods as wish to sail to this kingdom or river. — From Banjarmasin, dated the 30th of September 1733. — Article 3: One junk or wankang [type of vessel] shall be tolerated by the Company such that it may purchase pepper from the Banjarese up to its full loading capacity, but no more. When the junk or wankang that is permitted to purchase pepper cannot be fully loaded within this river, for fear of not being able to get out of this river without danger, it may bring the remainder of its loading with gontings [small boats] or other inland vessels outside, in order to take it in before the bank [sandbank]. 5. — To prevent all smuggling, when pepper is to be brought outside to the junk or wankang, notice must first be given to the chief officer of the Company that this pepper is for the permitted wankang, who shall then, according to his discretion, place one or two of his men there to see that this cargo is not handed over to any other vessels except to those that have been tolerated for the pepper trade. 6. — The Company shall also be free to place a vessel as a guard-watch by the junk that is permitted for the pepper trade, to see that it does not give pepper to its companions or others in or outside this river, under whatever pretext it might be, such shall not be permitted. From Banjarmasin, dated the 30th of September 1733.

text_translated_detailed: Men shall be placed there to see that this cargo is not handed over to any other vessels except to those that have been tolerated for the pepper trade. 6. — The Company shall also be free to place a vessel as a guard-watch by the junk that is permitted for the pepper trade, to see that it does not give pepper to its companions or others in or outside this river, under whatever pretext it might be, such shall not be permitted. When anyone loads pepper in gontings, wankangs, or other vessels that are closed and with which one could transport pepper, outside and besides the wankang that must be permitted annually, the chief officer of the Company shall have the shahbandar [harbor master] of Tatas called to him, and in his presence the pepper shall be removed from those vessels, confiscated, weighed, and divided: one half to the king to be paid at the contracted price, and the other half to the Company. When the shahbandar of Tatas or the one who is placed there in the king's name calls upon the chief officer of the Company regarding matters that cannot tolerate delay or waiting, and he does not appear immediately, then according to the discretion of the chief officer, the Company's servant may perform it alone, and the effect thereof shall be the same as if the king's people had been present, to prevent smuggling from occurring through delay and waiting, which would otherwise easily happen. Furthermore, the Company shall receive all the pepper that is found in this kingdom, the picul [unit of weight, approximately 125 pounds] or 125 pounds at 4¼ Spanish reals, both for the pepper and the king's [share].

' in't patria aan den gouverneur generaal en raden van India tot Batavia gedateert 14. ' 7ber 1731 en 30. ' Aug:s 1732. over den handel tot Banjermassing Van Banjermassing onder dato 30:' 7ber 1733. . Hoog Edele gestrenge groot Agtb=re Erntfeste, Manhafte en Wijt gebiedende heeren. — dat den peper insaam van Jaar tot Jaar is gedeclineert en de quantiteijt nooijt soo kleijn in een mousson is geweest als heden dat men van dien Corl heeft bemagtigt, is de rede de sterke vaart uijt China, die met besendings van drie Ja meer Jonken hier Jaarlijks komen en boven de Comp: om haare meerdere prijs, die, die handelaaren voor de peper geven geprefereert, en soude een heijlsaam middel sijn die volkeren van hier konde werden gehoude, waartoe alle middelen hebben in't werk gesteld, met beloften van in den aanstaande een vostigheijt te maken, en dese volkeren alle Jaaren te sullen versien, met soodanige Chineese whaaren als thans door die handelaaren werden aangebragt, maar men heeft bij de grooten deses rijx sulx niet kennen Obtineeren, die tot
text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin under date of the 30th of September 1733. — the copper wire and ironwork, weighing 50. pounds. A great quantity of bound rattan, all so burned and charred by the fire that not a single one of them was serviceable to be used. — A heap with rice burned, unusable. A heap with Cadjang burned. Ten hoops from a terracotta barrel. Furthermore, most of the military's chests and goods. This is what we have found, and we are duty-bound to report to Your Esteemed [authority], in order to remain [standing position] Esteemed Gentlemen, Your faithful servants [was signed] Jan van Hessel, Ditloff Nieustad and Jan Willem Lucasz [to the side was written] Banjarmasin on the 2nd of September 1733. — Respectful Answer to the Extracts from the general letters sent by the High Noble Gentlemen of the 17th [in the homeland] to the Governor-General and Council of India at Batavia dated the 14th of September 1731 and the 30th of August 1732, concerning the trade at Banjarmasin. From Banjarmasin under date of the 30th of September 1733. High Noble, strict, great Esteemed, Earnest, Valiant and Wise commanding gentlemen. — that the pepper harvest from year to year has declined, and the quantity has never been so small in a monsoon as it is now, that which one has obtained from that coast. The reason is the strong trade from China, which with shipments of three or more junks comes here yearly, and above the Company, because of their higher price, which those merchants give for the pepper, are preferred. And it would be a beneficial means if those peoples here could be retained, for which all means have been employed, with promises to make a provision in the coming [year], and to supply these peoples every year with such Chinese goods as are now brought by those merchants. But one has not been able to obtain such with the great ones of this realm, who [text continues]

From Banjarmasin under date 30th July 1733. — undoubtedly the Company shall yearly be able to carry away two or three ship-loads of pepper from here, if one maintains the contract as one has concluded it on the 26th of this month with the king and pangerang, remaining referred to the Company to establish a permanence so that pepper is fetched yearly with ships from here, then one shall certainly have more advantages than one has had until now, and one is thereby out of fear that no other nation shall come to settle here, as they shall not be tolerated by this king, but must depart from here with their business unfinished. — Amphioen [Amboyna cloth], clothing and some Nuremberg small wares one could sell here in small quantity, which is now abundantly brought by the Chinese, who through their continual voyage from Semarang provide these peoples here with it, and with a small profit because no heavy duties on their journey cause them to sell it here at a loss; we hope hereby to have fulfilled the intention of your High Excellency, greatly esteemed, to be permitted to remain /underneath:/ High

text_translated_detailed: Year 1733. From Banjarmasin dated 30th September 1733. — Daily Register kept by the Commissioners in the Banjarmasin trade, namely by the Merchant Christoffel de Marre and sub-merchant David Brouwer. On the 7th of March, through His High Excellency the Governor-General Mr. Dirk van Cloon, the papers and orders were handed to us so that we might conduct ourselves in this Commission according to them, we proceeded on board the ship Westerbeek. On the 8th, after muster had been taken, it set sail and we came outside the roadstead again to anchor to wait for the two Tanjong Pura. On the 9th, we set sail in the company of the Yacht the Friendship, the Tanjong Pura the Shamelessness and the Sick One. On the 22nd, we arrived at the roadstead of Banjarmasin; the Mate Barent Cuijper from Moscow, who had been stationed on the Tanjong Pura the Sick One, died. On the 23rd, the cargo of the ship Westerbeek was loaded into the two Tanjong Pura and the military personnel transferred into them. — Banjarmasin dated 30th September 1733. On the 24th of March we sailed with the Yacht the Friendship and the two Tanjong Pura toward the river of Banjarmasin. On the 25th, we came into the river of Banjarmasin and the boom keeper of Old Banjar came on board us, who informed us that he would give notice of our arrival to Tatas at the earliest. — On the 26th, while proceeding up the river, the sabandhar [local official] of Tatas came on board us and escorted us into the village; we understood from him that everything was in peace and quiet there. Three large Chinese junks passed by, which had already been here for 2 months. The Mate Casper Sijmon, who had been stationed on the Tanjong Pura the Shamelessness, died. On the 27th, an emissary who had been sent to Taijotonge

The first in this Commission was adorned around his neck with a red silk ribbon and carried the letter, which was protected from the sun with a parasol around which a yellow silk cloth had been wrapped, and went in a small vessel that brought us before the Sultan's residence. text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin dated 30th September 1733. In the middle, at the end of which we stepped into an antechamber of the residence, where the king, Pangerang Praboe Anum, the Captain of the Chinese, and a large number of the king's and prince's retinue came to meet us, and we handed over the letter and gift goods from the Governor-General and Council of India to that prince, while making a courteous greeting to him. Upon this the Sultan sat down on an alligator [chair] with his accompanying company, and a place being assigned to us across from the prince, some cannon that stood within the palisade fired 20 to 21 shots, whereupon the king opened the letter and having read it, 15 to 16 shots were fired again, which the prince indicated was done to the health of His High Excellency the Governor-General, which was answered with three cheers from the muskets of our accompanying soldiers, and thereby testified to the well-being of the king and the prince. While smoking cigars and consuming betel nut, we informed the prince of the purpose of our coming, to which he replied that he would need to speak with Pangerang Praboe Anum, and that this would be arranged at a later opportunity. After sitting a little longer, we took our leave with mutual courtesy and proceeded to the dwelling, where we arrived around six o'clock. In the evening around nine o'clock an emissary came to inform us that the Sultan would receive us the following day to speak about the letter and pepper trade.

text_translated_detailed: 1st of April. In the morning some emissaries came to fetch us to bring us to the Sultan, who, sitting in his inner court, was waiting for us at a table, where after a mutual compliment, we were placed together with Pangerang Praboe Anum on Chinese chairs. We proposed to the prince the intention of His High Excellency, that pepper be delivered to the Company alone, what advantage this would be for his land and people, to be assured of a steady fixed price and regular purchase. The prince replied that he would hold to what the previous Panabakan [local ruler] had promised, namely that a Chinese junk or wankang [type of vessel] would have to be provided to conduct the pepper trade here, and that he with Pangerang Praboe Anum was not in a position to make any change in this, as this had been done at that time with the knowledge and consent of all the inland regents. From Banjarmasin dated 30th September 1733. Upon this we requested His Majesty that all the great ones of this land might come together again, and that we might make known the intention of the Governor-General to all the princes so that one might have the opportunity to form a new contract with one another. The prince said he would consider this. During this opportunity we asked His Majesty what supply of pepper might be in the surrounding villages. The king replied that he did not know this, but addressed himself to the Captain Chinese, who answered 3,000 to 4,000 piculs [modern equivalent: approximately 180,000-240,000 kg], which did not accord with what we had been informed from other sources, which had stated that there were well 15,000 piculs, and rather more than less of the pepper supply. We pressed the prince strongly that the ship might obtain a speedy loading, and another be summoned in its place for greater frequency. The Sultan's answer was that the ship would be loaded within 3 months. We proposed this timeframe and requested that it be loaded as soon as possible, and that if there was more pepper than two ships could carry away, we received only this answer from Banjarmasin dated 30th September 1733 — the reply was: it is good, which

text_translated_detailed: From Banjarmasin under date 30th September 1733. For this land to be, the Honored Company be granted the pepper trade exclusively, which he granted to us, but that he had no village that produced pepper, but that the lands of Pangerang Manko, Nagare, and Singe Sari were the principal ones where this crop grew, but that he did not believe those princes would deliver their goods to the Honored Company, because the Governor-General and Council of India had not written to them, but that he firmly maintained that the king and Pangerang Praboe Anum would have all their pepper brought to us, but that their villages brought forth very little. He also told us that the present king had little command over his subjects, and if his orders did not accord with their interest, the common people would not observe them. The soldier Andries Hardendonk died. He passed through the village of Patas, Pangerang Aria de Coesoema, who was escorted by his brother-in-law Pangerang Praboe Anum, to make the journey to Chambawa and to be crowned king there. In the evening, Pangerang Praboe Anum returned and remained in this village. From Banjarmasin under date 30th September 1733. On the 8th of April, the Sultan and Pangerang Praboe Anum wishing to go back to Kajutange [Cirebon], requested an audience to take leave of that prince and to wish him a good journey, which was granted to us the following morning. On the 9th, early in the morning, we proceeded to the sultan and Pangerang Praboe Anum, who received us both kindly. This envoy also asked us when we would depart, since for a long time no pepper had been forthcoming, because the upper river lay mostly dry. We answered that when we could no longer obtain pepper, we would prepare ourselves for the journey first, and we requested of his kindness that he would be willing to seek an audience for us with Pangerang Marta so that we might take our leave from him. This prince granted us this in the afternoon. We proceeded to him and took a mutual polite leave from him after we had settled accounts with him regarding Penang tea and such. We proceeded to the dwelling. On the 10th of October, since no more pepper could be brought because of the dryness of the rivers, the two Commissioners found it good not to wait needlessly and to break up. This was signed C. de Marre and D. Brouwer. We undersigned declare that we have properly collated the foregoing letters and the attachments belonging thereto against their original and found them to be in accord therewith. Batavia, in the Castle, the 24th of December 1733. Adriaen Vesmaer, G. Keijser, V. Leeuw, L. Wijhoff, A. Creed.
